title: What is Parquet: a file format that stores data in columns instead of rows, which is much faster for analytics queries because you only read the columns you need (like reading only the "salary" column from a table with 100 columns).
keyPoints: Parquet is a columnar file format that stores values column by column instead of row by row.
Column pruning reads only the columns a query needs, cutting I/O by orders of magnitude on wide tables.
Predicate pushdown uses per-row-group min/max statistics to skip irrelevant blocks without decompression.
Same-type column values compress far better than mixed-type rows via dictionary and run-length encoding.
Parquet is self-describing: the file footer holds the full schema and statistics.
Parquet is write-once, read-many: it pairs with Delta Lake or Iceberg for ACID and updates.
It is the de facto format for data lakes and big-data engines like Spark, Trino, and Hive.

s1_definition.oneliner: Parquet stores data by column so analytics reads only the columns it needs, skips irrelevant data, and compresses far better than row formats.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Apache Parquet** – an open-source columnar storage file format optimized for analytical workloads.
- **Columnar layout** – storing all values of one column together, instead of all columns of one row together.
- **Column pruning** – reading only the columns a query needs, skipping the rest entirely.
- **Predicate pushdown** – using per-row-group min/max statistics to skip blocks that cannot match a filter.
- **Row group** – a horizontal partition of the data; each row group contains column chunks for every column.
- **Self-describing** – the file footer holds the full schema and per-column statistics.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a giant ledger with a hundred columns per transaction: account id, amount, timestamp, branch, device, and ninety-six more. A row-based file is like a book where each page holds one complete transaction with all hundred fields, so to total just the amount column you must flip through every page reading all hundred fields. Parquet is like re-filing the ledger so all the amounts sit together in one slim folder, all the branches in another. Now to total amounts you grab just the amount folder and ignore the other ninety-nine: far less reading, and since all amounts look alike they squash down tiny when zipped.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Row-Store vs Column-Store (Parquet)
  ───────────────────────────────────

  Row-Store (CSV)                  Column-Store (Parquet)
  ┌──────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ T1|15000|Oct|Mum │             │ txn_id: T1,T2,T3,... │
  │ T2|25000|Oct|Del │             │ amount: 15k,25k,...   │
  │ T3|30000|Oct|Blr │             │ date:   Oct,Oct,...   │
  │ (all cols per row)│            │ branch: Mum,Del,...   │
  └──────────────────┘             └──────────────────────┘

  SELECT SUM(amount):              SELECT SUM(amount):
  Read ALL columns :(              Read ONLY amount column :)
```

```text
  Parquet Scan Optimization
  ─────────────────────────
  Query: SELECT SUM(amount) WHERE date = '2024-10-29'

  Step 1: Column pruning
    -> Read only 'amount' and 'date' columns

  Step 2: Predicate pushdown
    -> Row group 0: date max = Sep  -> SKIP
    -> Row group 1: date max = Oct  -> READ
    -> Row group 2: date max = Nov  -> SKIP

  Step 3: Decompress + aggregate
    -> Only the surviving rows
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Apache Parquet is an open-source columnar storage file format built for analytics. Instead of storing data row by row, it stores values column by column, and that one change unlocks three big wins. Column pruning lets a query read just the columns it needs, cutting I/O by orders of magnitude on wide tables. Predicate pushdown uses per-row-group min/max statistics to skip entire blocks that cannot match a filter. And compression is far better because same-type column values encode efficiently via dictionary and run-length encoding plus a codec like Snappy.

Parquet is self-describing, with a footer holding the schema and statistics, which is why engines read the footer first to plan the scan. It integrates natively with Spark, Trino, Hive, and cloud warehouses. The trade-off is that Parquet is designed for write-once, read-many analytical use, not frequent single-row updates, which is why it pairs with lake table formats like Delta Lake and Iceberg for ACID and updates.

In a banking context at the National Bank of India, transaction history lived in partitioned Parquet in the data lake. A report needing total amounts read only the amount column and ignored dozens of other columns, and a report scoped to one date skipped every row group outside that date using min/max statistics.

The result was that analytical queries like per-branch quarterly totals were far cheaper in storage and far faster to run than they would have been in a row format.

Remember one sentence: Parquet stores data by column so analytics reads only what it needs, skips irrelevant blocks, and compresses hard.
